strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical problem: the large training memory overhead of teacher/discriminator-based one-step distillation methods for Real-ISR, and the inflexibility of fixed-step models.

The Self-Adversarial Distillation (SAD) scheme, which trains real and fake trajectories within a single model, is a sensible adaptation that (if verified) enables distillation of very large backbones (20B-parameter Qwen-Image) on a single GPU, which would be a valuable practical contribution to the community.

The Decoupled Timestep Condition (DTC) design is a clear, well-motivated architectural idea to avoid entangling current-noise and target-timestep information, and the ablation (Table 3, Fig. 5) shows a measurable and visually apparent improvement over naive timestep fusion.

Time-Aware Rectification is well motivated by a clear noise-dependent reliability argument, and the qualitative ablation convincingly shows it removes checkerboard artifacts common in distilled DiT-based SR models.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative comparisons are provided against several strong and recent baselines (OSEDiff, TSD-SR, SUPIR, DiT4SR, etc.) across three benchmark datasets and eight different metrics, plus an any-step evaluation table (Table 2) and qualitative step-scaling figure.
weaknesses: Table 2 shows that as inference steps increase from 1 to 30, almost all full-reference metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, FID) consistently get worse, not better, directly contradicting the paper's central claim that any-step sampling 'delivers even more superior performance as inference steps increase.' This is a significant unaddressed inconsistency that undermines a key selling point of the method; only marginal, inconsistent gains in NR metrics (MUSIQ/MANIQA/NIQE) are observed, and this tradeoff is not adequately analyzed or explained beyond a brief qualitative claim.

The main quantitative comparison (Table 1) is mixed rather than uniformly favorable: OSEDiff achieves better PSNR/SSIM on RealSR, and TSD-SR is superior on several perceptual/NR metrics (LPIPS, DISTS, MUSIQ, NIQE, FID) on DIV2K-Val, weakening the claim of consistent superiority over SOTA.

TEASR is built on a much larger and more recent backbone (Qwen-Image, 20B parameters) than the compared baselines (OSEDiff, TSD-SR, SUPIR, etc., typically SD/SD3-based), so improvements could partly stem from the stronger backbone rather than the proposed SAD/DTC/TAR contributions; no backbone-matched ablation or control experiment isolates the algorithmic contribution from the backbone-capacity confound.

Claims of training efficiency (single-GPU training of a 20B model) are not substantiated with concrete quantitative comparisons (e.g., peak memory in GB, wall-clock training time, throughput) against baseline distillation pipelines; only qualitative statements ('2-3x memory') are given without a corresponding table.

No ablation is provided for the core SAD component itself (the paper explicitly skips this, stating it degenerates to a multi-step model), leaving the necessity/effectiveness of the fake-trajectory adversarial mechanism versus, e.g., a simpler distillation loss, unverified.

The dual-branch conditioning architecture is directly borrowed from OminiControl with limited architectural novelty beyond the decoupled timestep assignment; overall the method is a combination of existing techniques (twin-trajectory self-adversarial distillation from TwinFlow/FACM, shortcut-model consistency objectives, DMD-style rectification) applied to Real-ISR, so the core novelty is more incremental integration than fundamentally new methodology.

No user study or perceptual preference evaluation is included despite perceptual quality being a central claim; no statistical significance or variance information (single run) is reported for the quantitative results.

Manuscript contains template artifacts (e.g., 'F. Author et al.', 'Abbreviated paper title') suggesting incomplete preparation, which slightly hampers assessment of final polish though not the core science.

strengths: The core motivation—eliminating auxiliary teacher/discriminator models during one-step distillation to reduce training memory—is practically valuable and the demonstrated scaling to a 20B-parameter Qwen-Image backbone on a single A100 is a notable engineering achievement if reproducible.
The any-step sampling capability (one unified model supporting 1 to 30 steps) addresses a real limitation of fixed-step distillation methods and is a useful practical contribution.

The proposed Decoupled Timestep Condition (DTC) is a reasonable architectural idea that avoids entangling two timestep signals into a single embedding, and the ablation in Table 3 shows it improves several fidelity metrics over naive timestep fusion.

Time-Aware Rectification (TAR) is a simple, well-motivated weighting scheme grounded in a plausible SNR argument, and the qualitative result (removal of checkerboard artifacts) is a concrete, visually verifiable benefit.
The paper provides reasonably broad quantitative comparisons across three benchmarks (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) against both multi-step and one-step SOTA baselines, plus qualitative figures.
weaknesses: The headline claim that TEASR 'consistently outperforms' SOTA is not well supported by Table 1: OSEDiff and TSD-SR frequently achieve better or comparable PSNR/SSIM/MUSIQ/MANIQA on RealSR and DIV2K-Val, and TEASR's advantage is largely confined to LPIPS/DISTS/FID on a subset of datasets—this is a much weaker and more mixed result than the abstract/intro imply.

The central 'any-step' selling point is undermined by the paper's own data: Table 2 shows that increasing sampling steps from 1 to 30 monotonically *degrades* all full-reference metrics (PSNR drops from 24.83 to 23.61, SSIM/LPIPS/DISTS/FID all worsen), directly contradicting the claim that 'our method generates more natural restoration results' as steps increase (Fig. 1) and that performance 'boosts' with more steps. Only marginal/noisy NR metric gains are observed, which is weak and potentially cherry-picked evidence (Fig. 4) given the quantitative trend runs opposite to the narrative.

No quantitative evidence (wall-clock training time, peak GPU memory, FLOPs/latency at inference) is given to substantiate the 'training-efficient' and 'single-GPU 20B training' claims beyond a single anecdotal sentence; a training-efficiency paper should report concrete memory/time comparisons against OSEDiff/TSD-SR-style multi-model training.

The ablation study is incomplete: the multiple auxiliary losses introduced (L_base, L_data, L_adv, L_rectify) are never individually ablated, and the SAD mechanism itself (the core contribution) is explicitly not ablated ('we do not conduct ablation study on it'), which is an unconvincing justification and leaves the necessity/contribution of several loss terms (especially the pixel-space fidelity anchoring) unverified.
No user study or statistical significance analysis is provided despite strong perceptual-quality claims, and the qualitative comparisons (Figs. 3-5) are limited to a handful of cherry-picked crops.

Missing comparisons to other recent fixed-step/any-step or scalable one-step SR distillation baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., HYPIR, OmniSR/OmgSR) that could be more directly comparable to the claimed contributions.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code/model release is mentioned, hyperparameters for the many loss weights (λ_cons, λ_lpips, etc.) and their sensitivity are not reported, and the training recipe (47,000 steps, batch size 1 with grad accumulation 2 on 2 A100s) seems quite limited for claims of robust generalization across 20B-parameter models.

Minor presentation issues: duplicate references (e.g., DDPM cited twice as [11] and [12]; DiffBIR cited twice as [21] and [22]), placeholder author name ('F. Author et al.') suggesting incomplete anonymization/formatting, and generally dense notation in Sec. 3 that could benefit from clearer intuition before the heavy equations.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing training overhead in one-step diffusion distillation for Real-ISR while retaining flexible any-step inference. Eliminating auxiliary teacher/discriminator models via self-adversarial distillation is a meaningful contribution that enables fine-tuning a 20B-parameter DiT (Qwen-Image) on a single A100, which is a strong and concrete efficiency claim.

The proposed Decoupled Timestep Condition (DTC) design is a sensible and well-motivated architectural refinement over prior fused-timestep consistency approaches, and the ablation (Table 3, Fig. 5) shows a clear, interpretable improvement in FR metrics and visual fidelity.

The Time-Aware Rectification (TAR) weighting scheme is intuitively justified (unreliable high-noise gradients vs. reliable low-noise gradients) and empirically shown to remove checkerboard artifacts common in distilled DiT-based SR methods, which is a useful practical finding.

The any-step sampling capability is a genuine practical advantage over fixed one-step distillation methods, letting users trade off speed and quality without retraining, and this is demonstrated both quantitatively (Table 2) and qualitatively (Fig. 4).

Extensive comparisons against strong recent baselines (OSEDiff, TSD-SR, DiT4SR, SUPIR, StableSR, DiffBIR) across three benchmarks (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) with both full-reference and no-reference metrics, plus qualitative comparisons, provide reasonably comprehensive empirical support.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains over the strongest one-step baselines (OSEDiff, TSD-SR) are mixed and often marginal or trade off across metrics (e.g., TEASR loses on PSNR/SSIM on RealSR, loses on several NR metrics like MUSIQ/MANIQA/NIQE across datasets), which somewhat weakens the claim of consistently outperforming SOTA; the paper's own text downplays these losses without fully engaging with why TAR/DTC do not universally improve NR metrics.

The efficiency claim (single A100, 20B model) is compelling but lacks a direct quantitative comparison of actual GPU memory/wall-clock training cost against competing one-step methods (e.g., OSEDiff, TSD-SR) trained under comparable settings; only step/model counts are shown in Table 1, not measured memory or time, which are the paper's central efficiency claims.

Ablation of the Self-Adversarial Distillation (SAD) component itself is explicitly skipped ('we do not conduct ablation study on it'), leaving the core contribution not directly validated against a natural alternative (e.g., a teacher-based distillation counterpart at comparable model capacity) to isolate whether SAD's benefits stem from the algorithm itself or other factors like backbone scale/data.

The evaluation for any-step sampling (Table 2) shows FR metrics monotonically worsening with more steps while NR metrics fluctuate only slightly, raising a question about whether increasing steps genuinely improves perceptual quality in a way current metrics can substantiate; a user study or more decisive NR trend would strengthen this key selling point.

Formulation details (Eqs. 6-11) are dense and some symbol reuse (e.g., overloading s for both the target timestep shorthand and later noise level in TAR) could confuse readers; reproducibility would benefit from clearer pseudocode for the full SAD training loop (not just inference in Algorithm 1) and explicit hyperparameters for loss weights (λcons, λlpips, etc.), which are not given in the main text.

Comparisons are made only at a single upscaling factor (×4); generality across other degradation settings or scales is untested, limiting the demonstrated scope of the claimed 'any-step' and 'training-efficient' framework.

strengths: Novel Self-Adversarial Distillation (SAD) formulation that performs teacher/discriminator-free one-step distillation within a single model, which is a meaningful practical contribution enabling distillation of very large (20B-parameter) DiT backbones on a single GPU — a capability existing DMD/ADD-style methods (requiring 2-3 co-resident models) cannot match.

The paper provides a rigorous theoretical derivation (Sec. 4 of supplementary) connecting the Time-Aware Rectification weight w(s) = (1-s)^2/s to a KL-divergence/score-matching argument, giving principled justification rather than an ad hoc heuristic, and this is validated with a sensitivity study over alternative schedules.

The Decoupled Timestep Condition (DTC) is a clean architectural idea that avoids entangling the two consistency-model timesteps into a single embedding, and ablations (Table 4, Fig. 6) show it clearly improves fidelity and reduces DiT-specific checkerboard artifacts.

Any-step sampling within a single trained model is a genuinely useful capability absent from prior one-step SR distillation methods (OSEDiff, TSD-SR, HYPIR), giving practitioners a speed/quality trade-off knob without retraining.

Broad empirical validation: quantitative comparison across 3 datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) with 8 metrics, qualitative comparisons, cross-backbone validation (Qwen-Image 20B and Z-Image 6B), and detailed training/inference efficiency analysis (memory, latency) support the practical efficiency claims.

Comprehensive ablations (SAD components, DTC, TAR) and supplementary materials (loss curves, training stability visualization, additional qualitative comparisons) improve confidence in reproducibility and soundness.
weaknesses: The claim that TEASR shows 'good performance scalability' with more sampling steps is only weakly supported: Table 3 shows PSNR and SSIM actually monotonically decrease as steps increase from 1 to 30 (PSNR 24.83→23.61, SSIM 0.7198→0.6837), with only marginal/mixed gains in no-reference metrics (MUSIQ nearly flat, NIQE improving slightly). This partially contradicts the headline narrative (Fig. 1/4, Sec 4.4) that more steps yield uniformly 'more natural' and higher-quality results, and the paper does not adequately explain or quantify this fidelity/realism trade-off.

Despite being framed as 'training-efficient,' the absolute peak training memory (77.69 GB, Supp Table 1) and inference memory (59 GB, Table 2) remain very large in absolute terms; the efficiency claim rests mainly on the relative overhead (15.6% increase vs baseline LoRA finetuning) rather than absolute accessibility, which could be stated more transparently as a limitation for typical single-GPU users without A100-class hardware.

The paper's claim of 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods' is somewhat overstated given Table 1: TSD-SR and OSEDiff frequently achieve the best or second-best MUSIQ/MANIQA scores, and OSEDiff has better PSNR/SSIM on RealSR; TEASR's advantage is concentrated in LPIPS/DISTS/FID rather than being uniform across all metrics.

No user study is conducted to substantiate perceptual-quality claims, relying instead on a small number of possibly curated qualitative examples (Figs. 3, 4, 6), which is a common but notable limitation for perceptual restoration papers making strong qualitative claims.

Training data is comparatively modest (LSDIR + first 10K FFHQ images, ~95K images total) relative to typical large-scale Real-ISR training pipelines; the paper does not discuss how this dataset scale interacts with using a 20B-parameter backbone, nor does it test generalization to more diverse or out-of-domain degradations/content (e.g., dedicated face benchmarks).

The dual-branch freezing scheme (freezing the noise-branch tokens, only tuning the condition-branch via LoRA) is adopted directly from OminiControl without ablating alternative split ratios or fully-tuned variants, leaving open whether the specific 50/50 branch split is optimal.

Code availability is left unspecified in the abstract ('Code:'), and given the complexity of the training pipeline (multiple interacting losses, timestep sampling schedules, TAR weighting), reproducibility would benefit from a public, well-documented implementation, which is not verifiable at review time.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: the heavy multi-model training memory overhead of existing one-step distillation methods (DMD/ADD-style) for Real-ISR, and the inflexibility of fixed-step distilled models.

The self-adversarial distillation (SAD) idea of folding teacher/discriminator/student roles into a single network via decoupled timestep conditioning is a reasonable and relatively elegant engineering solution, and the authors provide a DMD-style theoretical derivation connecting the proposed Time-Aware Rectification weight w(s) to the KL-divergence gradient.

Demonstrates that the framework scales to a 20B-parameter DiT backbone and trains with substantially less relative memory overhead than naive multi-model baselines, which is a nontrivial systems/engineering contribution.
Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val), multiple FR/NR metrics, qualitative comparisons, and an ablation isolating DTC and TAR contributions.
Any-step sampling without retraining is a useful practical capability relative to fixed one-step or fixed multi-step competitors.
weaknesses: The headline claim that performance improves monotonically with more sampling steps is directly contradicted by the paper's own Table 3: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS and FID all *degrade* as steps increase from 1 to 30 on RealSR, while NR metrics barely change or even worsen for LPIPS/FID. This undermines the central 'any-step, quality scales with compute' selling point stated in the abstract, intro and Fig. 1/4 captions, and the discrepancy is not adequately analyzed or reconciled.

Quantitative superiority over prior one-step methods (OSEDiff, TSD-SR) is mixed and often marginal: OSEDiff wins on PSNR/SSIM on RealSR, TSD-SR wins several NR/DISTS metrics on DIV2K-Val, and overall gains are small relative to the much larger backbone (20B vs 0.8–2B parameters) being used, making the comparison somewhat unfair in terms of capacity.

Despite the 'training-efficient' framing, actual resource requirements remain very high: peak training memory of ~60–78GB and inference latency of up to 10.3s for 30-step sampling, undermining the practical efficiency narrative; the 'single A100 GPU' claim is only meaningful for an 80GB A100 and still requires substantial hardware.

Core technical components are incremental recombinations of existing ideas: self-adversarial twin-trajectory distillation is explicitly adapted from concurrent works [3,28], the dual-branch conditioning follows OminiControl, and the DMD-style rectification follows prior DMD/TSD-SR work; the main novel element (TAR weighting and DTC) is a comparatively small modification.

The ablation study is thin — no ablation for SAD itself (explicitly skipped), no separate ablation of Ladv vs Ldata contributions, and only a 3-row table for DTC/TAR, limiting insight into which components actually drive the reported gains.

No user study is conducted despite heavy reliance on perceptual/NR metrics (MUSIQ, MANIQA, NIQE) that are known to be susceptible to hallucinated texture/artifacts; given the FR-metric degradation with more steps, it is unclear whether additional steps are adding genuine detail or distribution-shifted artifacts.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract lists 'Code:' with no actual repository link provided in the submitted manuscript text, and several training details (e.g., full degradation pipeline parameters, exact schedule for λ adjustments) are only partially specified.
Comparisons omit some recently cited one-step competitors (e.g., HYPIR) that are discussed in related work but not benchmarked quantitatively, leaving the state-of-the-art positioning incomplete.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical problem: existing one-step distillation methods for Real-ISR (DMD-style, ADD-style) require co-resident teacher/student/discriminator models, which severely limits scalability to large backbones. The proposed Self-Adversarial Distillation (SAD) approach that performs distillation within a single model is a compelling and well-motivated solution, enabling distillation of a 20B-parameter Qwen-Image backbone on a single A100 GPU, which is a strong demonstration of practical value.

The any-step sampling capability (unifying 1-step to 30-step sampling in a single trained model without retraining) is a nice and useful property that differentiates this work from prior one-step SR methods locked into a fixed sampling budget; Table 3 and Fig. 4 show a sensible quality/step tradeoff.

The Time-Aware Rectification (TAR) mechanism is theoretically grounded — the supplementary provides a clear derivation showing that the (1-s)^2/s weighting emerges naturally from the flow-matching score-difference relation used in the DMD-style rectification, rather than being an arbitrary heuristic. This is a genuine plus for soundness.

The Decoupled Timestep Condition (DTC) design is intuitive and ablated: separating tcur/ttar conditioning across dual branches instead of fusing them into a single embedding is shown (Table 4, Fig. 6) to improve fidelity, addressing a real limitation of prior shortcut/meanflow-style dual-timestep fusion schemes.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons against multiple relevant one-step (OSEDiff, TSD-SR) and multi-step (StableSR, DiffBIR, SUPIR, DiT4SR) baselines across three datasets (RealSR, DRealSR, DIV2K-Val) with a comprehensive metric suite (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/DISTS/FID/MUSIQ/MANIQA/NIQE), plus memory/latency benchmarking (Table 2, supplementary Table 1) and a second backbone (Z-Image) to show generality across model scale.

Reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 4, Fig. 6) isolating DTC and TAR contributions, plus a TAR schedule sensitivity analysis in the supplementary that supports the chosen weighting over alternatives.
Clear writing and figures illustrating the qualitative benefits (e.g., reduced checkerboard artifacts, more natural detail with more steps) that support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: Quantitative superiority is modest and mixed: TEASR is not uniformly best across metrics/datasets (e.g., OSEDiff/TSD-SR sometimes match or exceed TEASR on some FR or NR metrics such as MUSIQ), and improvements on RealSR/DRealSR PSNR/SSIM over the strongest baseline are often small margins that may not be highly significant given only single-run results without variance/confidence intervals.

The core one-step model is built on top of a 20B-parameter backbone (Qwen-Image) while baselines (OSEDiff SD2.1 0.86B, TSD-SR SD3-m 2B) use far smaller backbones; this makes head-to-head comparisons somewhat unfair, since gains could partly stem from backbone scale/capacity rather than the proposed SAD/DTC/TAR contributions. A more scale-matched comparison (e.g., TEASR trained on SD2.1 or a similarly small backbone) would better isolate the algorithmic contribution.

Despite claiming 'training-efficient' status, absolute training memory (77.69 GB per Table 1 in supplementary) is still very large in absolute terms (only single-GPU feasible on an 80GB A100); the efficiency claim is relative to naive multi-model distillation on the same huge backbone, but this is a somewhat narrow framing since most practitioners would not attempt to distill a 20B model in the first place. The paper could better contextualize efficiency gains against realistic use cases at more common backbone scales.

The training and inference latency at higher sampling steps (10.31s per image at 30 steps in Table 2) is far slower than lightweight one-step baselines (OSEDiff at 0.15s), so the 'any-step' flexibility trades off substantial wall-clock efficiency at higher quality settings — this practical cost/benefit tradeoff deserves clearer discussion.

The paper's framing of 'eliminating auxiliary models' is somewhat overstated since the method still requires two forward passes per rectification step (dual conditioning calls to vθ within the same network) and multiple loss terms (Lflow, Lcons, Ldata, Ladv, Lrectify) that add training complexity; the reduction is in parameter/memory footprint rather than compute complexity, which should be more precisely delineated.

Ablation for SAD itself is skipped ('we do not conduct ablation study on it' since without SAD it degenerates to a general multi-step model) — while understandable, this leaves the core novel training paradigm without direct empirical isolation against a comparable one-step alternative trained with the same backbone/data, weakening the causal claim that SAD specifically (versus just having more capacity/data/compute) is responsible for one-step quality.

Some visual comparisons (Fig. 3, Fig. 6) are selective and it's unclear if failure cases exist; no discussion of common failure modes or degradation types where TEASR underperforms is provided beyond generic 'slight trade-offs under extreme conditions.'

Reproducibility: code is promised but link is missing at submission stage; several hyperparameters (e.g., the tan-based λflow/cons weighting) are somewhat ad hoc and their sensitivity is not analyzed in the main paper (only briefly in supplementary for TAR, not for other loss weights).
